checks.claim: Key: only the tablet's bubbles are a new substance; an effervescent antacid (aspirin, sodium bicarbonate, citric acid) fizzes from an acid-base reaction making carbon dioxide once water reaches it
Wrong choices: bubbles in boiling water are water vapour (a change of state, no new substance), so 'only boiling', 'both' and 'neither' are all wrong
checks.note: The first tiny bubbles before a full boil are dissolved air escaping, also not a new substance, so no wrong choice becomes right.

checks.claim: Context: bubbles from a non-boiling liquid are a clue to a new substance, not proof; boiling bubbles are water turned to gas
Key: an air-activated hand warmer (iron powder, salt, water, charcoal, vermiculite) heats because the iron oxidises (rusts) fast in air, an exothermic reaction; salt speeds it
Second source for the reaction, the salt as catalyst, and the airtight outer wrapper
Wrong choice: salt dissolving in water gives off heat. NaCl's enthalpy of solution is about +3.87 kJ/mol, slightly endothermic, so the context's 'gives off no heat at all' is true
Wrong choices: grains rubbing (friction) and stored sunlight are not the heat source; the heat is the oxidation reaction
Context: stays hot for hours (about 50-55 C for 8-12 hours); slow rusting of a gate is not felt as warmth
Key: limewater (saturated calcium hydroxide, 'slaked lime') is clear and turns milky as carbon dioxide forms insoluble calcium carbonate, a precipitate

Second source: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3(s) + H2O, 'milky' from precipitation of insoluble calcium carbonate; calcium hydroxide is traditionally called slaked lime, so 'the lime dissolved in the water' is a fair simplification
Breath turns limewater cloudy within 20-30 seconds through a straw (fits 'within a minute')
Context: calcium carbonate is the stuff of chalk and limestone and practically insoluble
Wrong choices (trapped bubbles, mist from breath, dust) are not the cause of the lasting milkiness
Key: copper turns blue-green by reacting with oxygen, carbon dioxide, water (and in cities sulfur dioxide) from air and rain, forming a patina
checks.note: Real roof patina is a mix of basic copper carbonate, sulfates (brochantite) and near the sea chlorides. The context names only oxygen, carbon dioxide and water; that is incomplete but not false, and the key ('air and rain') covers sulfur from the air too. No fix needed.

checks.claim: Second source: green patina is mixtures of copper chlorides, sulfides, sulfates and carbonates depending on the air; takes many years
Context: the patina adheres tightly and protects the copper beneath; patinated copper roofs last over a century
Wrong choice: moss and algae make the green. Copper is toxic to moss and algae (copper strips are sold to keep them off roofs), and the green is a copper compound
Wrong choices: rain washing off the shine, sunlight fading the colour; neither makes a green compound
New copper is reddish-orange

Key: a glow stick lights because two liquids (hydrogen peroxide and a phenyl oxalate ester with a fluorescent dye) react once bending breaks the inner glass vial and shaking mixes them (chemiluminescence)
checks.note: Grokipedia puts the peroxide in the outer tube, Wikipedia puts it in the vial; the question names neither, so it survives either way.

checks.claim: Second source: bending breaks the inner container, the solutions combine, energy excites the dye; the reaction releases energy mostly as light, so little heat
Context and wrong choice: glow-in-the-dark materials absorb light and re-emit it slowly (phosphorescence); chemiluminescence needs no light first, so 'daylight it soaked up' is wrong
Wrong choices: heat from the snap, static sparks from shaking; neither is the light source
Glows for hours (4-12 hours standard)
Stem: fresh sweat has almost no smell. Eccrine sweat is odourless; apocrine secretion is an odourless fluid
Key: skin bacteria (Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus hominis) break sweat components down into smelly compounds (thioalcohols, short-chain fatty acids)
Second source: 'Sweat itself doesn't smell'; the water, salt and fat of sweat mix with bacteria and cause odour (supports the context's 'mostly water with a little salt and fat')
Wrong choices: drying sweat concentrating a smell, salt left behind, sweat soaking into cloth; none makes the odour, which comes from bacterial breakdown products
checks.note: Salt is odourless or at most faint (Wikipedia Sodium chloride infobox).

checks.claim: Hematite is iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3; massive/crystalline specimens are black to silver-grey and metallic; it leaves a reddish-brown streak
Key: the streak is the colour of the mineral's own fine powder rubbed on unglazed porcelain, so the powder is the same mineral ground fine (a physical change)
Wrong choice 'powder from the tile': the plate is about Mohs 6.5-7, harder than metallic hematite (5-6.5), so the mineral, not the tile, is ground off
Wrong choices: a new substance made by rubbing, a different red rock inside; both wrong, the streak is hematite itself
Context: streak often differs from the lump's colour and geologists use it to tell minerals apart; so a colour change is a clue, not proof

Stem: two white powders (barium hydroxide octahydrate, sold as white crystals or crystalline powder; ammonium chloride, a white crystalline solid) stirred in a flask freeze it to a wetted wooden block
checks.note: RSC: 'the water on the base freezes causing the watch glass or wooden block to freeze to the flask'. Colours: https://www.thermofisher.com/order/catalog/product/203140010 and https://grokipedia.com/page/Ammonium_chloride

checks.claim: Context: temperature drops to about -20 C
Context: products are ammonia, water and a new solid (barium chloride dihydrate); damp red litmus turns blue from ammonia vapour
Key: some reactions take in heat (endothermic), so the surroundings cool
Wrong choice 'Yes, some reactions give off cold': cold is not a substance; thermal energy flows only from warmer to cooler, so the reaction draws heat in rather than giving cold out
checks.note: This is the standard 'cold flows' misconception lure; the context explains why it is wrong. Not defensible as right in a science frame.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'reactions only give off heat' and 'only melting makes things colder': this reaction itself (and evaporation, dissolving ammonium nitrate) disproves both

unit_notes: All eight questions check out. Minor notes only: the copper patina context names oxygen, carbon dioxide and water, while real roof patina is often mostly sulfates (from sulfur dioxide) or chlorides near the sea; incomplete but not false. Sources disagree on which glow-stick liquid sits in the glass vial; the question does not say, so it is safe.
